name: Zhurong rover
headline: China's first Mars rover drove south for a year, went to sleep for winter, and never woke
story: At 07:18 Beijing time on 15 May 2021, still 14 May by the clock in Greenwich, the Tianwen-1 lander settled onto the smooth plains of southern Utopia Planitia. A week later, on 22 May, the rover Zhurong rolled down its ramp onto Martian soil, making China the second nation to operate a rover on another planet.

It was designed for 90 Martian days. Instead it drove south for nearly a year, its wheel tracks traced from orbit by NASA's HiRISE camera, and covered 1,921 meters. In May 2022, with dust storms dimming its solar panels and winter closing in, controllers put it into a planned dormancy. They expected it to wake around December.

It never did. In April 2023 the program's chief designer said dust had most likely piled up on its panels, leaving too little power to restart. HiRISE images from September 2022 and February 2023 show the rover in the same spot. Zhurong still stands there, a short drive south of the silent lander that carried it down.

facts.label: First drive
facts.value: 22 May 2021, 02:40 UTC, onto the Martian surface

facts.label: Went dormant
facts.value: May 2022; expected to wake around December 2022, but never did

images.caption: 6 June 2021, seen by NASA's HiRISE: the Tianwen-1 lander inside a dark blast pattern from its descent, with the Zhurong rover just to the south.
11 March 2022: Zhurong, the dark speck at center, among pale wind-shaped ridges after roughly 1.5 kilometers of driving south.
March 2022, September 2022, February 2023: between the last two views the rover did not move. It had gone to sleep and would not wake.
